transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-06-14 15:00 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Morgan Patel (Redwood, AE); Samir Kohli (Redwood, SE); Taylor Nguyen (Apollo, Prod Eng); Jules Romero (Apollo, Infra Lead); Priya Shah (Apollo, SecOps)

Summary:
Apollo Dynamics is evaluating Redwood for a mixed deployment (hosted initial pilot -> Dedicated/Private for regulated workflows). Main concerns: defined RTO/RPO for inference services, fallback behavior during region outages, cost/latency tradeoffs for multi-region routing, and compliance for EU data residency and HSM-backed keys. They want a perf pilot + security pack before exec approval.

Topics covered:
- Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private fit for telemetry and PII
- Multi-region steering and expected latency impact for failover
- Fallback policies: model downscale, read-only cached responses, circuit breaking
- SLA expectations and what triggers credits/rollbacks
- On-prem/VPC constraints and KMS/HSM integration
- Pilot scope: traffic slice, success criteria, timeline

Action items (captured):
- Morgan to send pricing + pilot T&Cs and brief cost model
- Samir to share benchmark harness and sheet with test cases
- Priya to share traffic profile and PII list

Transcript body:
[00:00] Morgan (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Just to orient — this is a 45-ish minute discovery to understand your reliability and failure-mode constraints and see if Redwood Hosted or Dedicated/Private is the right fit. Samir from our SE team will cover technical details.
[00:34] Taylor (Prod Eng): Thanks. Quick context: we power a B2B chat assistant that handles both general and regulated customer support for EU clients. Peak qps is around 120 rps and we care a lot about the 95th and 99th percentiles; acceptable p50 is ~120ms, p95 target for completions around 450ms.
[01:12] Jules (Infra): From infra side we need to know what happens if a region goes down — do you fail over to another region, and how much latency jump should we expect? Also cost impacts.
[01:37] Samir (SE): Great. So Redwood supports multi-region routing; you can define a primary region with automatic failover to fallbacks. The latency delta depends on model size and distance; typically p95 will increase by 2x–4x if you fail to a distant region, but you can mitigate with smaller model variants or cached prefixes.
[02:18] Priya (SecOps): When you say cached prefixes, is that KV cache? We have strict rules around any cached PII.
[02:40] Samir (SE): Right, sorry, KV cache — I sometimes say K-V cash in calls — it's the key-value attention cache for in-flight tokens. Redwood supports prefix caching with TTLs and you can opt-out for PII-heavy prompts. For Private mode we can map cache persistence to your storage and manage retention.
[03:18] Taylor: If we fall back to a smaller model to preserve latency, what's the fallback chain look like? Do we lose semantics?
[03:38] Morgan: We usually recommend a three-tier fallback: primary (best-quality, highest cost), fallback-1 (quantized variant or smaller architecture), fallback-2 (very small fast model or cached response). And you can set thresholds — e.g., if p95 latency > 700ms or error rate spikes >2%, trigger fallback to variant.
[04:11] Jules: And is that automatic or does it require redeploy?
[04:20] Samir: Automatic. The runtime supports circuit-breakers and automated routing rules. You can do A/B or canary rollouts and have automatic fallback policies per route. We log events and expose tracing so you can audit fallback triggers.
[04:55] Priya: About audit — we need immutable audit trails for inference decisions and SSO integration. Do you support SAML/SSO and paged audit logs?
[05:12] Morgan: Yes, SAML/SSO and RBAC are supported; audit logs are exportable to your SIEM and we support long-term retention as an add-on. For Private deployments you can keep logs on your side.
[05:40] Taylor: On SLAs — our procurement team wants a clear RTO and credits calculation. What SLA levels do you offer for Hosted vs Dedicated?
[05:58] Samir: Hosted has best-effort availability with published performance targets; Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and latency SLOs depending on commit. Typical guarantees for Dedicated are 99.9% with recovery-time objectives specified in the contract, and we offer credits that scale with downtime and missed latency windows. Exact numbers are contractable.
[06:40] Jules: If we need EU-only processing for some endpoints, can we pin routes to EU-only Dedicated capacity?
[06:52] Morgan: Yes — you can route traffic by policy to region-restricted Dedicated pools. For Private we can deploy into your EU VPC or on-prem. You can also pin model versions for compliance.
[07:18] Taylor: We worry about stealth degradations — say a node in the pool is slow, causing tail latency increases. How do you monitor and proactively route away?
[07:36] Samir: We have per-node health checks and continuous latency sampling. The router can circuit-break a node and re-route; there's also per-token throttling and backpressure to allow graceful degradation. You can set routing policy to favor low-latency vs low-cost.
[08:10] Priya: KMS/HSM — we need to use our HSM for root keys. Is that supported?
[08:21] Samir: For Private deployments yes; we integrate with customer KMS/HSM (PKCS#11/HSM providers) and for Dedicated we can support customer-managed keys with restricted export. Hosted supports envelope encryption with customer-managed KMS in many cloud providers.
[08:55] Taylor: How does failover affect token billing and cost — if we fail to a different region and use a larger model, are we charged differently?
[09:10] Morgan: Yes billing follows the model variant and region. We surface cost impact in logs and in the Console; during pilot we can model cost with expected failover frequency to estimate blended unit cost.
[09:40] Jules: For pilot we want to replicate a partial outage scenario and observe behavior — can you run a simulated region outage and show metrics?
[09:55] Samir: Absolutely — we can run chaos-style simulations in a controlled pilot. We'll capture latency, error rates, fallback activations, and KV cache hit ratio. We'll put results in a shared sheet.
[10:28] Taylor: Quick question on mode of fallback — do you ever serve stale cached completions for reduced cost? We may prefer stale but safe responses for some endpoints.
[10:42] Morgan: That's configurable per route. You can set a tier that returns last-known-good completion when model is unavailable, or return an error. Many customers use stale-cached replies for readonly knowledge queries.
[11:03] Priya: On data residency — Private deployment to EU is expensive. Can you guarantee bounded replication windows for logs and KV cache?
[11:18] Samir: You can configure asynchronous replication windows or disable replication; for strict residency we recommend Dedicated or Private where the control plane is in-region. For Hosted we have region-locked offerings but you'd need to sign the data residency addendum.
[11:55] Taylor: In terms of metrics we need — we track p50, p95, p99, error-rate, cold-starts, and model switch counts. Will your console surface per-route metrics and token-level cost?
[12:12] Morgan: Yes — Console provides per-route dashboards with token cost, latency histograms, and traces. You can also export raw telemetry.
[12:40] Jules: About on-call — if something happens at 2am we need on-call rotation. Do you offer SRE support for Dedicated?
[12:52] Morgan: We offer enterprise support packages with 24/7 SRE escalation for Dedicated customers and runbook alignment sessions.
[13:20] Taylor: We're also evaluating Anthropic's offering — they have multi-region but fewer fallback knobs. Why should we pick Redwood?
[13:36] Samir: Two quick differentiators: our runtime supports continuous batching and KV cache controls that allow more predictable tail latency, and our deployment abstraction gives you consistent tooling across Hosted/Dedicated/Private so you don't rebuild runbooks when you move mode.
[14:05] Priya: Any specific compliance artifacts you can share now? We need SOC2, ISO27001, and pen test summary.
[14:18] Morgan: We'll send the SOC2 and ISO packages and an executive summary of the latest penetration test. For deeper questions we can set an NDA-driven security review.
[14:47] Taylor: Let's talk concrete reliability numbers. For Dedicated, what RTO can we contractually expect if an entire region fails?
[15:01] Samir: Typical contractual RTO is in the 5–15 minute range for automated failover to a warm standby depending on your topology. Hot-active multi-region reduces that to roughly sub-5 minutes but at higher cost. We'll propose a topology matrix in the pilot doc.
[15:34] Jules: Warm standby meaning we keep standby capacity in second region — is that reserved and billed?
[15:44] Morgan: Yes, reserved capacity or burst capacity options — both are available. Reserved is cheaper if you commit, burst is pay-as-you-go.
[16:10] Taylor: If we run in Private hashed into our VPC and something goes wrong, who has access to logs?
[16:21] Priya: (interjects) We need to ensure only our security team has the keys.
[16:28] Samir: For Private deployments the customer owns the control plane keys and audit logs; Redwood staff access is restricted by contract. For Dedicated we can set RBAC to limit access and require access requests via your SSO with approvals.
[16:55] Taylor: For the pilot success criteria — we want: 95% of requests under p95 target, no data exfiltration concerns, and documented rollback/playbook. Is that reasonable?
[17:10] Morgan: That's fine. Typical pilot success looks like: pass perf targets on a 10% traffic replay, confirm failover behavior, complete a security review, and agree on SLA terms.
[17:36] Jules: About rollback — if the new model causes quality regressions in production but meets latency, how do we handle automatic fallback to previous model?
[17:48] Samir: You can define model pinning and automatic rollback on quality regressions measured by your eval suite or by signal thresholds. Redwood Optimize can monitor prompt-sets and trigger alerts or automated rollback.
[18:16] Taylor: Our QA will want to run a regression harness. Can you run automated evals against historical prompts?
[18:28] Samir: Yes we can. We'll run an eval set from your sample traffic and surface quality delta. That's part of the pilot tasks.
[18:50] Priya: If we need to keep the KV cache disabled for PII endpoints, do you support mixed routes where some endpoints have cache and others don't?
[19:02] Samir: Yes — cache behavior is per-route. You can define a route for PII with cache disabled and a public route with aggressive prefix caching.
[19:30] Taylor: We also have a procurement constraint — any SLA must include clear crediting formula. Can you share a template?
[19:42] Morgan: We'll include a sample SLA clause in the materials we send. It will show uptime, latency SLOs, and credit percentages.
[20:05] Jules: On multi-region routing, how does session affinity work if you're failing over mid-session? We need to keep context for chats.
[20:18] Samir: Good point — we keep KV cache pinned to a session; if we failover mid-session, KV cache may not be available unless you replicate it or accept a cold start. We support optional cross-region replication with configurable windows. If you can't tolerate context loss, you'd want hot-active or immediate replication configured.
[20:55] Taylor: That replication sounds like a source of cost. Can you show cost delta for hot-active vs warm standby vs cold failover?
[21:10] Morgan: We'll include a cost matrix in the pricing doc. It will show compute/replication costs and example scenarios.
[21:40] Priya: Another security question — we need branch-level RBAC and ability to revoke keys instantly.
[21:50] Samir: Our platform supports RBAC at route and team level and immediate key rotation APIs. For Private you can centrally control keys.
[22:18] Taylor: For the pilot testcases we want three scenarios: normal load, region outage failover, and increased error rates that trigger fallback. Can you run all three?
[22:32] Samir: Yes — we can simulate all three and produce a report showing latency, fallbacks triggered, and resource utilization. We'll need a replay of representative traffic.
[22:58] Morgan: We'll send a template for the traffic sample and a short checklist for the pilot.
[23:10] Jules: On reporting — during failover do you mark requests with failover reason in traces? We want to be able to orient on why traffic hit fallback.
[23:24] Samir: Yes — traces will include routing decision, fallback reason, and model variant used. You can filter in Console.
[23:50] Taylor: Is there a hard limit on how many fallback variants you can define?
[23:59] Samir: No hard limit, but operationally most customers use 2–3 tiers.
[24:20] Priya: A question about legal — if we run a Dedicated pool and you host in our AWS account, who bears compliance?
[24:33] Morgan: For Dedicated in your account you control the infra and Redwood provides the software layer; responsibilities are split in the contract. We'll coordinate legal precisely.
[24:58] Taylor: Performance: for our longest context windows (~8k tokens) what's expected p95 on a TGI-style model if using Dedicated A100/SSDs?
[25:14] Samir: Rough numbers — on Dedicated A100-ish hosts p95 for 8k context can be 700–1,200ms depending on batching; quantized variants will be faster but may reduce quality. We'll measure this in the pilot.
[25:46] Jules: If we want to instrument custom metrics, can we push traces to our ingest?
[25:55] Samir: You can forward metrics/traces to your Prometheus/Datadog/Elastic endpoint. We support OTLP and common exporters.
[26:20] Taylor: For the runbook, can you provide a sample incident playbook for region outage?
[26:32] Morgan: Yes — we'll share a playbook template that includes runbook steps, escalation contacts, and rollback triggers.
[26:58] Priya: About pen test — if we ask for the pen test artifacts, is that public or NDA?
[27:08] Morgan: Usually the full report is shared under NDA; we'll include a summary in the initial pack.
[27:32] Taylor: For timeline — we need to get pilot results to procurement by early July. Is that feasible?
[27:44] Samir: Feasible if we start the pilot this week and you provide traffic sample and access details. Pilot duration typically 2–3 weeks for perf + security checks.
[28:12] Jules: What's the expected ramp for us if we go from 10% traffic to full cutover — any recommended guardrails?
[28:23] Samir: We recommend step-based ramp (10% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100%) with quality checks at each step and automatic rollback thresholds. Also use canary rate limiting to bound blast radius.
[28:50] Taylor: One more: during degradation do you offer partial functionality flags — e.g., degrade to single-turn responses vs multi-turn?
[29:03] Samir: Yes — route-level feature flags allow you to return simplified responses or limit token length.
[29:30] Priya: Are there any public incidents or postmortems we can review?
[29:42] Morgan: We have anonymized postmortems; we'll include an anonymized incident summary showing fallbacks and lessons learned.
[30:12] Taylor: For billing forecasting, can you provide a unit-cost simulator?
[30:22] Morgan: Yes — we'll include a simple cost simulator in the pilot packet that takes your traffic profile and shows expected costs under different topologies.
[30:46] Jules: Regarding regional failure modes — do you have recommended SLO wording we can use in procurement?
[30:56] Samir: We'll draft suggested SLO language for inclusion in the contract (uptime, latency windows, credits).
[31:20] Taylor: If we sign Dedicated, how long does deployment typically take?
[31:29] Morgan: Depending on region and commit, Dedicated can be ready in 2–6 weeks. Private on-prem is longer (6–12 weeks) due to integration.
[31:58] Priya: For the security review we'll prepare a list of questions — who should receive them?
[32:08] Morgan: Send to me and I will route to our security team. We'll respond and if needed set a security deep-dive.
[32:28] Taylor: On-call access — how do we rotate privileges for vendor SREs?
[32:36] Samir: We require approval workflows; access is time-limited and logged. For Dedicated we can require jumpbox access through your SSO.
[33:05] Jules: Any major caveats we should be aware of?
[33:12] Samir: Two caveats: cross-region replication adds cost and complexity; also model-downscale fallback can change semantics so quality monitoring is key.
[33:38] Taylor: Ok. Let's talk next steps — can you outline what you'll send after this call?
[33:46] Morgan: We'll send: pricing + pilot T&Cs, SOC2/ISO pack, a pilot checklist and cost simulator, and a proposed schedule for the 2-week pilot. Samir will add the benchmark sheet and suggested testcases.
[34:10] Priya: We'll compile the traffic sample and PII mapping and aim to send by 2027-06-17.
[34:22] Samir: I'll prepare the chaos scenarios and bench harness, and can run a small smoke run once we have the sample.
[34:50] Taylor: One more tiny thing — do you have an example of failover metadata in traces? Would be useful to poke at a real trace format.
[35:04] Samir: Yes — I'll include an example trace snippet and the Console screenshot showing fallback reasons.
[35:30] Morgan: Great. Anything else from Apollo?
[35:36] Jules: Not from me.
[35:39] Priya: No.
[35:42] Taylor: No, that's it. Thanks.
[35:46] Morgan: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with materials. Recap: pilot start ASAP, materials by next week, security review to follow.
[36:05] (call ends)

Links/References mentioned:

End of transcript.
